style: Write natural, concise UI Chinese as a native product designer would; never translate word-for-word.
Use full-width Chinese punctuation (，。：；？！“”（）) inside Chinese sentences. Keep the source's ellipsis “…” and the middle dot “·” as they are.
Put a half-width space between Chinese characters and adjacent Latin letters or digits (e.g. “3 个任务”, “导出为 PDF”). No space between Chinese and full-width punctuation.
Buttons and menu items are short verb phrases without a final full stop (e.g. “新建笔记”, not “新建一条笔记。”). Keep a final full stop only where the English sentence has one.
Address the user neutrally; avoid “您” and “你” unless the sentence needs a subject, and then use “你”.
Keep placeholders such as {count} or {title} exactly as written, and reorder them freely to fit Chinese word order.
Keep keyboard symbols and key names (⌘ ⌥ ⇧ ⌃ ↵ Esc Tab Enter Space) and shortcut letters unchanged.
Lowercase English source text (for example search keywords or inline hints) does not need to stay lowercase in Chinese.
Number words that follow a Chinese word still take the space: “标题 1”, not “标题1”.

terms.note: Task labels. Distinct from note tags; never translate as 标签.
Saved table/board/list views and task views.
Tasks spaces: ongoing areas you keep up rather than finish.
Lanes like Now, Next, Later that tasks are sorted into by hand.
An item captured into the Inbox (noun); as a verb, 记录.
Inbox bucket for things not needed now.
macOS wording; acceptable on all platforms for now.
Feature name: the daily page with today's note and tasks. Never translate as 每日笔记.
Inbox bucket and tray section for captures still to decide on. Use the same word everywhere it means this.
Move a capture into a note or folder. Distinct from Archive (归档).
